Concise operational definition: Immediate, present-focused report of thermal sensation or comfort, without further interpretation or domain-specific disruption.
Explanation, attribution or comparison of why conditions feel hot, humid, muggy, sticky, dry or otherwise uncomfortable.
Heat-related difficulty sleeping or disruption of night-time routines without clinical diagnosis or medical-risk framing.
Domestic routines, family, companionship or pets under heat, without explicit animal-health risk or institutional provision.
Heat-related work or commuting burden, including PPE discomfort, productivity loss or travel inconvenience, without medical framing.
Heat experienced during self-directed walking, exercise, leisure or travel, emphasizing personal constraints or adjustment.
Heat experienced in structured events, venues, crowds or queues where organised conditions or operations are central.
Venting, humour, exaggeration, celebration or savouring used to regulate or socially communicate affect; excludes clinical mental-health burden.
Personal cooling through air conditioning, fans, shade, staying indoors or seeking cooler spaces, rather than institutional provision.
Cooling or relief through food and beverages, including cold drinks, chilled food and ice cream.
Heightened susceptibility or exposure among older adults, children, unhoused or chronically ill people, marginalised groups or outdoor workers.
Heat-related illness, dehydration, overheating, rescue or mortality risk affecting pets or wildlife.
Explicit physical symptoms, heat illness, dehydration, fainting, nausea, emergency care or symptom-specific medical advice.
Explicit anxiety, depression, psychological distress or mental-health-system strain extending beyond everyday venting or humour.
Population-level mortality, hospitalisation, epidemiological burden or pressure on health services.
Heat alerts, risk reminders or preventive guidance, including hydration, check-ins and avoiding exposure.
Unequal heat exposure, housing conditions or cooling access framed through resource distribution, marginalisation, responsibility or justice.
Links urban form, materials, greenery, infrastructure or planning to heat exposure or cooling conditions.
Heat-driven electricity demand, grid stress, outages, cascading impacts, resilience measures or energy-system response.
Institutional cooling provision, service rescheduling, emergency operations or governance decisions responding to heat.
Explicitly attributes current heat or related extreme weather to climate change or global warming.
Debate, scepticism, denial, conspiracy, persuasion or contestation concerning climate-related interpretations of heat.
Situates heat within long-term trends, climate background or seasonality without explicit causal attribution.
Frames heat alongside drought, wildfire, smoke, flood or other interacting hazards and cascading risks.
